claim.pdf_says: 1) I-O status = 10. A sequential READ statement is attempted and no next or prior logical record exists in the physical file because:  [p255] a)  NEXT was specified or implied and the end of the physical file has been reached, or  [p256] b)  PREVIOUS was specified and the beginning of the physical file has been reached, or  [p256] c)  a sequential READ statement is attempted for the first time on a file described as optional and the physical file is not present.
claim.markdown_says: a) NEXT was specified or implied and the end of the physical file has been reached, or b) PREVIOUS was specified and the beginning of the physical file has been reached, or c) a sequential READ statement is attempted for the first time on a file described as optional and the physical file is not present.
claim.why_it_matters: Section 9.1.13.4 rule 1) has three parallel alternative sub-items a), b) and c) in the PDF, each its own list item (a) at the foot of printed page 225, b) and c) at the head of printed page 226). The markdown (specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 11336) collapses all three into a single run-on paragraph placed entirely before the anchor. The list structure that marks them as three independent 'or' alternatives is destroyed, b) and c) are attributed to the wrong page, and any tooling that enumerates sub-items of a rule sees one item where the standard has three. Content is present, so nothing normative is lost - only structure and page attribution.

verdict.reasoning: Independently rendered both PDF pages at 300 dpi and read the printed glyphs. The claim's factual description of both sources is ACCURATE: PDF page 255 (printed 225) ends 9.1.13.4 rule 1) with exactly one sub-item, 'a) NEXT was specified or implied and the end of the physical file has been reached, or', as its last line of body text before the '(c)ISO/IEC 2023 225' footer; PDF page 256 (printed 226) opens with two further hanging-indent sub-items, 'b) PREVIOUS was specified and the beginning of the physical file has been reached, or' and 'c) a sequential READ statement is attempted for the first time on a file described as optional and the physical file is not present.' The markdown at specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 11336 does join all three onto one line ahead of the anchor. But this is not a content discrepancy, and it is rejected on three of the stated grounds. (1) Nothing is missing: I compared the joined markdown line word-for-word against the rendered glyphs of all three PDF sub-items and it is verbatim, including both 'or' connectors and the terminal period. (2) No choice indicator is lost. Looking at the printed glyphs myself, the PDF markers are the literal two-character sequences 'a)', 'b)', 'c)' set at the sub-item hanging indent - not bullets, not an autonumbered construct - and all three of 'a)', 'b)', 'c)' survive as literal glyphs in the markdown line, in order, each still immediately preceding its own alternative. A reader or tool sees three lettered alternatives joined by 'or' either way. (3) The remaining difference is page-break furniture plus paragraph re-wrapping, which the mandate excludes: the sub-list physically straddles the 225/226 leaf, so the transcription had to land the straddling text on one side of the page anchor, and it chose to keep the rule's alternatives together with the rule stem rather than split mid-list. Meaning is identical - the three alternatives, their letters, their 'or' disjunction and their scope under rule 1) all read the same. The claim itself concedes 'nothing normative is lost - only structure and page attribution.' The 'tooling that enumerates sub-items' argument does not survive inspection either: this markdown file does not use CommonMark list syntax for lettered sub-items anywhere - the immediate siblings in the same section (9.1.13.5 rule 2) a/b/c at lines 11352-11356, rule 3) a/b/c/d at lines 11360-11366) are plain three-space-indented paragraphs, and 'a)' is not a markdown list marker, so no list structure existed to destroy; the file's convention is one paragraph per sub-item and the only deviation here is that a page-break-straddling group was not re-split. Cosmetic transcription tidiness at most, not a spec-fidelity defect, and not something that could mislead a conformance implementation of I-O status 10.
